audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Russian passage is verbatim in the held scanned of Arzumanov & Sanginov 1988 at PDF pp. 13-14 = book pp. 126-127, §20, exactly as cited; the Baizoyev & Hayward domain quote is verbatim in the archive.org text (Lesson 1). (2) The deciding source is a 1988 pedagogical grammar, corroborated by a 2004 pedagogical course; both give an explicit, detailed and mutually consistent rule (final stress on the base and on derivational/plural suffixes; izofat, pronominal enclitics, -ro, indefinite -e, copula clitics, conjunction clitics and -mi unstressed; verbal me-/bi- stressed). This matches the catalog's classification fixed-strict final, domain word (clitics excluded, verbs set aside per the domain quotation). sources.quote: "The situation with stress in the Tajik language is considerably simpler. Here too it is a force (dynamic) stress, but immobile, i.e. fixed. The most general rule here can be taken to be that stress usually falls on the last syllable of the word taken with zero marking, i.e. in its base form (nominal parts of speech not extended by affixes, infinitives of verbs, gerundive-participial forms, adverbs). For example: khona', kito'b, devo'r, kabu'd, doda'n, rafta'n, ijroshuda', takhmina'n."

sources.quote: 'The position of stress in Tajiki is very regular. In all Tajiki words, except for verbs, stress falls on the last syllable of words. If a suffix is added to a word, the stress falls on the suffix: baro'dar - baroda'ri ... In verbs, stress usually falls on the first syllable: 'giriftam ... inflectional suffixes are never stressed: kor'gar -> kor'garam; ki'tob -> ki'tobam; the indefinite article ... -e, is never stressed.'

sources.quote: No rule for word-stress placement is stated. Stress appears only incidentally: vowel reduction of /i u a/ 'in unstressed open syllables', with stress-marked examples /beˈɾaXm/ 'merciless', /biˈɾinʥ/ 'rice' (both final-stressed disyllables), and Table 1 durations of stressed vs unstressed /i u/. Describes the Bukhara (Uzbekistan) dialect, not literary Tajik.
